summary: Asks the network community for comments on how socket names should be structured. Two layouts are offered for the 32-bit socket number, one almost entirely arbitrary and one with defined fields. It answers a request made at the February 1971 meeting in Illinois.

plainLanguage.summary: A socket number is like a mailbox address. This note shows two ways to build that address and four ways to hand the addresses out, then asks the network community which it prefers.

questions: how should socket numbers be structured
what socket name layouts were proposed in 1971
subtitle: Two layouts for 32-bit socket names and four schemes for handing them out, offered for comment in 1971.

tldr.problem: Hosts on the early network needed a way to name sockets so that two users could find each other and be confident they were talking to the right party.
tldr.mechanism: The RFC offers two socket name structures, an almost entirely arbitrary 31-bit number or a 24-bit user ID with a 7-bit tag, each ending in a one-bit gender, and weighs four ways to assign and look up names.
tldr.outcome: It makes no decision. It asks readers to reply through the standard RFC process, and the unit metadata shows it was updated by RFC 147.

today: RFC 129 is a request for comments rather than a specification, and the unit metadata lists RFC 147 as an update to it.

sections.title: Two Socket Name Structures
sections.content:
The RFC answers a request made at the February NWG meeting at the University of Illinois for comments on suggested socket name structures. Two structures are presented, and both are 32 bits long and end in a one-bit gender.

  • Structure 1: 31 bits of arbitrary value, then the gender bit.
  • Structure 2: a 24-bit user ID, a 7-bit tag, then the gender bit. This ties sockets to users rather than to processes.

The note then gives three ways the arbitrary number in structure 1 might be assigned: users pick it themselves, a logger picks it dynamically and records it in a directory, or it is assigned outside a logger but may be issued by a logger to the far party.
sections.plainLanguage: Think of a mailbox number. One design lets you choose almost all of it yourself. The other begins with your own user ID and adds a small tag for each socket.

sections.title: Schemes One to Three
sections.content:
The running example is User A at Host A connecting to User B at Host B at an agreed time, and the two issues are addressing and security.

Scheme 1 lets a user pick any 32-bit socket identifier. The least significant bit gives the socket's gender, 0 for read and 1 for write, and no more than one active socket may carry a given identifier at a host. It is simple and reasonably safe in a non-malicious setting, but conflicts are possible and each pair of users needs a prior private agreement.

Scheme 2 has the host choose the identifier, with a Network Directory service relating an identifier to the name of the user operating it. It allows symbolic addressing but is cumbersome and not absolutely secure, because a socket can be deactivated and its name later reused.

Scheme 3 uses user identifiers assigned by the home host, with a list of 256 sockets the user may operate. If both hosts enforce the assignment, misconnection is prevented and there can be no naming conflict between users, and arrangements can be made openly. Some systems may be unable to ensure user ID integrity.
sections.plainLanguage: You can choose your own mailbox number, ask the post office to assign one and look it up in a directory, or get a number that begins with your own personal code. Each way trades convenience against certainty about who you are reaching.

sections.title: Scheme Four: Naming Programs
sections.content:
A fourth scheme starts from a different view of the network: connections are made between programs, so programs rather than users should be identified. Programs need a fixed, unique identifier known to their remote users and perhaps to a local logger, and if a program allows several concurrent connections it also needs a range of variable identifiers, sensibly grouped in a contiguous range and tied to individual network connections.

The note gives Rand's Network Services Program as an example. Its socket names use a 24-bit administratively assigned program number, a 7-bit multiplex code that is normally chosen randomly, and a gender bit. Structure 1 can hold this and other naming schemes layered on its arbitrary field.
sections.plainLanguage: Here the mailbox number names the program that owns it, plus a small extra number for each separate conversation. A user's identity can be sent later, once a service has been requested.

fields.name: User ID
fields.desc: User identifier assigned by the home host.

fields.name: Tag
fields.desc: Distinguishes sockets belonging to the same user.

fields.name: Gender
fields.desc: Least significant bit: 0 for read, 1 for write.
